meta.title: Who really said "If there is a God, he will have to beg my forgiveness"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Reported as scratched in German on a cell wall at the Mauthausen concentration camp. The report is real and repeatedly documented; no photograph of the inscription has been located and it is unclear whether the cut survives. The author is unknown.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'If there is a God, he will have to beg my forgiveness'?
meta.ogDescription: Reported from a wall at Mauthausen, in German. What is documented is the report, not the wall. The author has never been identified.

answer.label: An unknown prisoner at Mauthausen — reported, not photographed
answer.authorDates: Mauthausen concentration camp, Austria · author never identified
answer.sourceLine: The words are reported to have been scratched into a wall at the Mauthausen concentration camp in Austria, in German: ‘Wenn es einen Gott gibt muß er mich um Verzeihung bitten.’ The report is old and repeated in serious places, but it is a report: we could locate no photograph of the inscription and no camp-archive record of it, and we have not been able to confirm whether the cut survives; the person who cut it has never been identified. We rate this attributed — more than a rumour, less than a document.

source.excerpt: Wenn es einen Gott gibt muß er mich um Verzeihung bitten.
trail: The work most often cited as carrying this inscription is not a book but a film: Rückkehr unerwünscht – Das Konzentrationslager Mauthausen, a 1987 Austrian documentary directed by Anneliese Wiesler (SHB Medienzentrum) that is screened for visitors at the Mauthausen memorial. It shares its title with a 1978 book by the Mauthausen prisoner Joseph E. Drexel (1896–1976) — edited by Wilhelm Raimund Beyer — and the two are easily confused; we found nothing that links Drexel’s book to this inscription. We were not able to view the film ourselves, so we give no timecode and do not present its wording as confirmed the film ↗.

The inscription is quoted in the peer-reviewed literature — Jennifer Lassley, ‘A Defective Covenant: Abandonment of Faith among Jewish Survivors of the Holocaust,’ International Social Science Review 90:2 (2015) — which places it on the prison-cell walls at Mauthausen and states plainly that the authorship is unknown the article ↗.

It also circulates steadily in German public writing, where it is treated as a prisoner’s inscription at Mauthausen without further citation — for instance in a column by the German journalist Heribert Prantl, which locates it on a barrack wall and offers no source beyond that the column ↗.

What we could not establish: any photograph, any camp-archive catalogue number, any surviving cut in the stone, or a first-hand witness we could read directly. The commonly repeated explanation — that the marks were visible until the walls were re-plastered when the site was prepared for visitors — is itself an unsourced claim, and we do not repeat it as fact.
source.excerptNote: The German as it is usually given. The English rendering most people know — ‘he will have to beg my forgiveness’ — is a translation of this, and a slightly sharper one than the German requires: um Verzeihung bitten is simply ‘to ask forgiveness.’
source.rightsNote: We deliberately state no rights status. The words are an anonymous inscription made under Nazi imprisonment by a person who has never been identified and who in all likelihood did not survive; there is no author, no publisher and no estate to point to, and an anonymous work of that period has no clean term to quote. The modern books and articles that carry the line are separately in copyright as texts, but the sentence itself is not theirs. Quote it as what it is — a prisoner’s words, reported — and say so. This is not legal advice.

author.name: An unknown prisoner at Mauthausen
author.heading: About the person who wrote it
author.metaLine: Mauthausen concentration camp, Austria · identity unknown
author.bio: Nothing is known about the writer. Mauthausen held political prisoners, Jews, Roma, Republican Spaniards, Soviet prisoners of war and many others; roughly 90,000 people died there. The sentence is in German, which narrows very little — German was the language of the camp, and prisoners from across Europe wrote in it. It is often said online that the writer was a Jewish prisoner. That may be true; we have found nothing that establishes it, and we would rather leave the person unlabelled than invent an identity for them.

misattribution.heading: What travels with it, and what to correct
misattribution.intro: Nobody is trying to steal this line — there is no famous name to steal it for. The errors are of a different kind: the camp gets swapped, the wording drifts, and the reporting gets described as harder than it is.

items.why: Every substantive account places the inscription at Mauthausen, in Austria. If you repeat this line, name Mauthausen.

The German is one sentence; the English is not fixed. You will see ‘If God exists, he will have to beg my forgiveness,’ ‘he must ask me for forgiveness,’ and ‘he’d better apologise.’ All are renderings of the same German, and none of them is the original wording, because the original wording is German.

The line is regularly posted alongside claims that the carving is preserved, or shown with a photograph of some other wall. We could locate no photograph of this inscription and no archive record of it. What exists is testimony that someone saw it.

Very widely stated, including in the version of the question that brought us here. It is plausible — Mauthausen held thousands of Jewish prisoners — but we found no source that identifies the writer’s name, nationality or religion, and we could find no first-hand witness named anywhere in the reporting chain.

misattribution.truthLine: An anonymous prisoner’s inscription, reported from Mauthausen and quoted in the scholarly literature, where the authorship is stated to be unknown. The report is documented; the wall is not the article ↗.

context.heading: Why it resonates
lead: It reverses the direction of a very old sentence. Prisoners were expected to ask forgiveness; the theology of suffering asks the sufferer to submit. This turns the whole arrangement round and hands the accusation back, and it does it in eleven words of German, scratched into a wall.

It is also not quite atheism. ‘If there is a God’ leaves the question open — the writer is not denying that anyone is listening, but setting a condition on what listening would now mean. That is a much harder thing to say than simply saying there is no God, which may be why the line has outlived the wall it was cut into.
context.detailsSummary: What we can and cannot show
detailsBody: Documented: the inscription is quoted in peer-reviewed scholarship on faith after the Holocaust, located at Mauthausen, with authorship stated as unknown.

Documented: a German form of the sentence circulates consistently — ‘Wenn es einen Gott gibt muß er mich um Verzeihung bitten’ — which is what you would expect of a real inscription rather than an English-language invention.

Reported but unverified by us: that a 1987 documentary screened at the Mauthausen memorial, Rückkehr unerwünscht – Das Konzentrationslager Mauthausen (dir. Anneliese Wiesler), carries this inscription. We were not able to view the film ourselves.
Not established: the writer’s name, nationality or religion; the date of the inscription; its exact location within the camp.
Not located: any photograph, any camp-archive catalogue number, any surviving physical trace.
We have set this to 'attributed' rather than 'verified' on that basis. If a reader can point us to a photograph or an archive reference, we will change it.
context.pull: The report is documented. The wall is not. Those are different things, and the difference matters here.
